title: Tourism careers
titleCn: 旅游专业选课与职业规划咨询

paragraphs.text: Part three.
You will hear a discussion between a student called Leon and a careers counselor called Mrs. Winters.
First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five.
Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.
Hi, Mrs. Winters. As you know, I'm interested in studying tourism next year, so I'm after some information on the courses available in Wellington.
How have you come to that decision?

Well, it's a growing industry, isn't it? So the long-term prospects for this area have got to be pretty positive, I'd say. Also, when I've visited other countries myself, I haven't always been happy with the service I've received, which has made me want to find out how that could be improved. I don't know. I've been thinking about it for a long time now, I guess, though I've never actually had a job related to it.
And I see from your CV that you sent me anyway that you've had some summer employment, so those skills will transfer.
Mm-hmm.
I imagine you've gained some experience in drafting formal letters and reports from this role with the legal firm.
Um, actually, no. In fact, I spent most of that summer photocopying in a back room with not much contact with the other staff.
Oh, well. You've worked for the local bank in the budgeting department, I see, so that will help.
I hope so. My experiences overseas might be of some use to me too. I'm not very good at waiting, so standing in long queues was annoying.
Uh-huh.

But I've definitely become more accepting of other cultures through seeing firsthand that there are other ways of doing things and have gained a lot of respect for those who travel on their own. I had my best mate with me, and we did most things together.
Well, now, let's get your study plan sorted out, shall we?
Yes. Right. I've been thinking of going to Queen Alexandra University.
They offer a BCA in marketing with a specialty in tourism, and that would be your best bet as it prepares you for all aspects of the industry.
Mm. I've been reading about how a good degree can lead on to jobs in ecotourism.

Yes, ecotourism was attracting increasing numbers of graduates for a while there, though I know that the number of jobs offered has fallen off recently. How keen are you on that, though? Because to go that route long term really requires you to be completely dedicated to the cause. And because it's a new field, no one knows right now quite how environmental tourism is going to develop or whether it will last at all.

Well, I'm pretty keen, but I'll think about it some more. Thanks. And I guess the alternative to Queen Alexandra University is to go to the Central Polytechnic instead. I'm not sure which would be best as far as my chances of getting employment at the end of it go. My cousin went to the Polytechnic, and she said that it's the opposite of what you'd think. The fees are actually higher there than at the uni because the courses are full of work experience, so you pay for your materials.
Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty.
Now listen and answer questions twenty-six to thirty.

So that's the public sector. I'm also interested in a private provider, the Sir William Rolleston College. Actually, I'm thinking of the certificate in travel and business. The website says that's an accelerated course. What does that mean exactly?
Oh, it's pretty high powered because it teaches three subjects in a short time frame.
Right. I phoned someone about cultural tourism, and that has a course in spoken Japanese, so you can communicate with your tourists.

Yes, that's an interesting one. And have you looked into tourism operations? That one's a bit different because there's an extra session on learning to treat minor injuries and accidents that your tourists might suffer.
Hmm. But to be an event organizer, would I qualify for admission to that certificate, or do you need to get workplace experience first?
You'd be okay because they accept the school-leaving certificate or the equivalent in work experience, so there'd be no problem there.
Ah.
And finally, the computer certificate at William Rolleston has a module on how to interact with clients and deal with their requests, like when you're making reservations in a travel agency.
Hmm, that's interesting.
Well, you have a lot of choices open to you, Leon. Good luck making a decision.
That is the end of part three. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to part three.
